# Introduction {#sec-intro}

According to Gallup, 22% of American workers worried technology would make their job obsolete in 2023, up seven percentage points from 2021 [@Gallup2023]. Concerns about automation were evident years earlier. In 2017, the Pew Research Center reported that 72% of Americans surveyed worried about a future in which robots and computers could perform many jobs currently done by humans [@Pew2017]. These concerns may partly reflect the economic consequences of job displacement, which has been associated with large and persistent earnings losses for affected workers [@CouchPlaczek2010].

In their study, [@CouchPlaczek2010] found that displaced workers’ earnings fell by more than 30% initially, remaining about 15% lower six years later. The burden of those earnings losses depended in part on local prices. As demonstrated by @Moretti2013, the same income could support different living standards in different places. This study therefore used purchasing power, income adjusted for differences in local price levels, as its outcome, and examined its association with county task groups.

To connect these automation concerns to local economic conditions, the study needed a measure of the tasks performed in local labor markets. The framework for this measure followed Autor’s work on task based technological change across three studies. @Autor2003 first showed that computers substituted for routine tasks while complementing non-routine ones, which made it possible to identify work more susceptible to automation. @AcemogluAutor2011 later extended the framework by treating tasks as the unit of production, with different skill groups competing to perform them. @AutorDorn2013 then applied the approach to local labor markets. Areas initially concentrated in routine work experienced employment polarization, with employment rising at both ends of the wage distribution and falling in the middle.

Earlier work focused on employment and wages rather than purchasing power and used broader labor market geographies than counties. This left open whether county task groups were associated with purchasing power and whether that relationship appeared in dollar levels or proportional terms. This study examined that question using a county level panel from 2008 through 2023, excluding 2020, with 11,983 observations across 840 counties. Throughout the study period, the analytical sample covered more populous counties that represented a large majority of the U.S. population, reaching approximately 84% in 2023 [@census_popest2023]. County employment was classified into the four task groups shown in @fig-taskframework and described further in @sec-data.

```{python}
#| label: fig-taskframework
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "**The Four Task Groups.** Each occupation falls in one cell of the Autor (2003) task framework. Routine tasks follow explicit rules that a machine can be programmed to carry out; non-routine tasks require judgment, adaptability, or in person interaction. Cognitive tasks work primarily with information; manual tasks work with physical objects and people. Occupation groupings follow Autor and Dorn (2013). Non-routine cognitive, outlined with a dashed border, is the reference group omitted from the regression."
%%R -w 8.5 -h 6 -u in -r 150 -b transparent
quad_df <- data.frame(
  group = c("Non-Routine Cognitive", "Non-Routine Manual", "Routine Cognitive", "Routine Manual"),
  col = c(2, 2, 1, 1),
  row = c(2, 1, 2, 1),
  examples = c("Management, engineering,\nteaching", "Food service, care work,\ncleaning",
               "Clerical, sales,\nclaims processing", "Production, assembly,\nmachine operation"),
  is_reference = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE)
)
quad_df$group_label <- gsub(" ", "\n", quad_df$group)
quad_df$linetype <- ifelse(quad_df$is_reference, "dashed", "solid")
quad_df$linewidth <- ifelse(quad_df$is_reference, 1.3, 0.9)

box_w <- 0.42; box_h <- 0.42

col_headers <- data.frame(
  col = c(1, 2),
  label = c("Routine", "Non-Routine")
)
row_headers <- data.frame(
  row = c(2, 1),
  label = c("Cognitive", "Manual")
)

ggplot(quad_df) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin=col-box_w, xmax=col+box_w, ymin=row-box_h, ymax=row+box_h,
                color=group, linetype=linetype, linewidth=linewidth),
            fill="#FCFCFB") +
  geom_text(aes(x=col, y=row+0.14, label=group_label, color=group),
            fontface="bold", size=4.6, lineheight=0.95) +
  geom_text(aes(x=col, y=row-0.20, label=examples), color="#52514E", size=3.1, lineheight=1.0) +
  geom_text(data=col_headers, aes(x=col, y=2.65, label=label),
            fontface="bold", size=4.3, color="#0B0B0B", inherit.aes=FALSE) +
  geom_text(data=row_headers, aes(x=0.52, y=row, label=label),
            hjust=1, size=3.6, color="#0B0B0B", lineheight=0.95, inherit.aes=FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values=TASK_COLORS, guide="none") +
  scale_linetype_identity() +
  scale_linewidth_identity() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0.05, 2.55), ylim=c(0.5, 2.85), clip="off") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.margin=margin(10, 10, 10, 10),
        plot.background=element_rect(fill=NA, color=NA),
        plot.title=element_text(face="bold", size=13, hjust=0.5)) +
  labs(title="The Four Task Groups")
```

We estimated a panel regression of purchasing power on the task groups, controlling for poverty, unemployment, and population. Year indicators absorbed year specific changes, and standard errors were clustered by county for repeated observations of the same place. For policymakers and economic development agencies, this offers a way to distinguish counties that look similar on poverty and unemployment but differ in what residents can afford. Diagnostic checks supported a log specification, while random forest and neural network models assessed whether more flexible models captured additional structure. The primary finding was that a one percentage point shift from non-routine cognitive to non-routine manual work was associated with approximately \$846 less purchasing power at the panel mean (95% confidence interval, ±\$38). Task groups therefore captured differences across counties that poverty and unemployment did not. @sec-analysis describes the modeling strategy and diagnostics.
